title: Hand of Straights
description:
You hold cards with integer values `hand`. You want to arrange **all** of them into groups of exactly `groupSize` cards, where each group consists of consecutive values (like `3,4,5`).

Return `true` if such an arrangement exists, `false` otherwise.
hints: If the count of cards is not divisible by groupSize, fail immediately.
The smallest remaining card has no choice: it must start a group. Remove that whole run of consecutive values from the counts.
Count values in a hash map, iterate the distinct values in sorted order, and for each value with count c > 0 subtract c from the next groupSize values; if any of them has fewer than c, fail.
signature: def isNStraightHand(self, hand: List[int], groupSize: int) -> bool:
approach:
**The smallest card still in hand is forced: it can only be the first card of a group.** So count the cards, visit the distinct values in increasing order, and whenever a value `v` still has `c` copies, all `c` of them must start groups `v, v+1, ..., v+groupSize-1`. Subtract `c` from each of those values; if one of them has fewer than `c` copies, no arrangement exists.

**Why it works (exchange argument):** in any valid arrangement the minimum value begins its group, and groups starting at the same value are interchangeable, so taking all `c` of them at once loses nothing. After removal the remaining multiset is independent of how we labelled the groups, so the greedy choice is never regretted.

Processing by distinct value (not card by card) keeps the work at O(distinct * groupSize), and the `Counter` makes `count[v]` return 0 for absent values without a special case. A min-heap over distinct values gives the same complexity and is what you would use if values arrived online.

**Common mistakes:** forgetting the divisibility check, sorting the whole hand and simulating removals from a list (O(n^2)), and not skipping values whose count has already dropped to 0.

**Interview follow-ups:** Values up to 10^9: does your solution depend on the value range? (No, only on the number of distinct values.) Return the groups themselves? (Emit a tuple each time you consume a run.) A variant where groups need only be consecutive *or* equal, like a rummy hand? (Then it is a DP over counts, greedy no longer suffices.) Allow jokers that fill gaps? (Track a wildcard budget.)
